title: PETER'S ASIAN BUSINESS & FINANCE BRIEFING - Thursday 27 August 2026, 06:00 Hong Kong
text:
Thursday’s Opening Call
Hang Seng (Hong Kong) Projected Open: 25,667 +14 points +0.1%
Nikkei 225 (Japan) Projected Open: 66,300 +38 points +0.1%
Quick Summary - 4 Things To Know Before Asian Markets Open
The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge rose more than expected last month. July’s personal consumption expenditures price index — a monthly report detailing changes in prices of goods and services and the Federal Reserve’s preferred metric of inflation — showed a month-over-month and year-over-year increase of 0.2% and 3.7%, respectively. Both figures were 0.1% above what economists polled by Dow Jones had expected. However, core PCE, which excludes food and energy prices, came in as expected with a gain of 0.2% on the month and 3.3% annually.
Nvidia reported better-than-expected fiscal second quarter results and issued revenue guidance that topped estimates. The world’s most valuable company reported revenue of US$96.2bn for the quarter to the end of July versus US$92.2bn expected. The company, which sits at the centre of the artificial intelligence world and has grown exponentially on the back of the AI boom, forecast sales of US$108bn plus or minus 2% for the current quarter, beating Wall Street estimates of US$104bn. The stock rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday.
Australia’s July inflation reading came in hotter than expected, underscoring stubborn price pressures and sharply increasing the likelihood of another Reserve Bank rate hike before year‑end. The trimmed mean measure rose 3.6% from a year earlier, beating forecasts of 3.5%, while core inflation accelerated to 0.5% on the month, from 0.3% a month earlier. That is a pace economists say is inconsistent with the RBA’s goal of returning inflation to the 2–3% target band.
US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s bond market intervention is pulling in the opposite direction to the Federal Reserve’s battle against inflation, big investors have warned ahead of chair Kevin Warsh’s first appearance at the Jackson Hole symposium at the end of the week. Wall Street has widely criticised Bessent’s surprise move last week to “at least double” the Treasury’s purchases of long-term US government debt, with investors saying it could undermine the agency’s credibility and work against the Fed’s ability to tame this year’s inflation flare-up.
Nvidia Earnings More Than Doubles, Beating Estimates
Nvidia reported better-than-expected fiscal second quarter results and issued revenue guidance that topped estimates. The world’s most valuable company reported revenue of US$96.2bn for the quarter to the end of July versus US$92.2bn expected. The company, which sits at the centre of the artificial intelligence world and has grown exponentially on the back of the AI boom, forecast sales of US$108bn plus or minus 2% for the current quarter, beating Wall Street estimates of US$104bn. Net income in the quarter more than doubled to US$53.95 billion, or $2.22 per share, from US$24.76 billion, or $1.87 per share in the year-ago period. The stock rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday, after CFO Colette Kress said on a call with analysts that Nvidia expects fiscal 2028 revenue growth of 70%, while analysts were expecting 44%.
Data centre revenue, which relates to the company’s core AI chip business that has been the primary driver of its growth, was US$89bn, up 117% year-on-year. Net income rose to US$59.7bn, while gross margin was 75%. But Nvidia said it expected a gross margin of about 74% for the current quarter, slightly below the 75% analysts expected.
The company’s chips have been used to build and serve the most advanced AI models, and increasingly Nvidia is providing financial support through backstops and other arrangements that allow new AI data centres to get funded and built. Almost four years since the launch of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Nvidia is still seeing massive growth, with revenue more than doubling in the latest quarter from US$46.7 billion a year earlier. CEO Jensen Huang has also mobilised outside capital. Earlier this month, Nvidia said it was working with a Wall Street consortium to assemble a US$500bn funding package, enabling customers to access financing from groups including Apollo Global, KKR, Brookfield, BlackRock and Goldman Sachs.
Markets Await Warsh’s Jackson Hole Speech
Investors are warning that US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s surprise intervention in the bond market is working at cross‑purposes with the Federal Reserve’s fight against inflation, setting up an awkward backdrop for chair Kevin Warsh’s debut appearance at the Jackson Hole symposium. Bessent’s decision to “at least double” long‑dated Treasury purchases — an effort to pull down yields after borrowing costs hit a 19‑year high — has drawn sharp criticism on Wall Street, where many argue the move risks undermining the Treasury’s credibility and easing financial conditions just as Fed officials are signalling the need for tighter policy. The intervention has had only a muted impact on yields so far, but if successful it would lower mortgage rates and other borrowing costs, effectively juicing the economy at a moment when the Fed is contemplating rate hikes to cool an inflation flareup. Analysts say the manoeuvre has unsettled not only investors but potentially members of the FOMC, leaving Warsh with a delicate balancing act when he addresses the Kansas City Fed’s flagship conference on Friday.
US Weighs More Trade Measures Against Canada After Retaliation
The US is discussing additional trade penalties against Canada after Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled dollar-for-dollar retaliation to new tariffs imposed on Saturday. Next steps may include higher tariffs and other actions, a White House official said. Meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford called for a truce in his war of words with Donald Trump but backed Canada’s plan to retaliate. The Canadian government announced that it would double its existing counter-tariffs on US steel and aluminium products to 50% and apply new 50% duties to other US products, affecting US$20 billion worth of annual US exports to Canada.
Australia’s Unexpected Inflation Overshoot Boosts Rate-Hike Case
Australia’s July inflation reading came in hotter than expected, underscoring stubborn price pressures and sharply increasing the likelihood of another Reserve Bank rate hike before year‑end. The trimmed‑mean measure rose 3.6% from a year earlier, beating forecasts of 3.5%, while core inflation accelerated to 0.5% on the month, from 0.3% a month earlier. That is a pace economists say is inconsistent with the RBA’s goal of returning inflation to the 2–3% target band. The data pushed the Australian dollar to a three‑month high and sent bond yields climbing, with money markets now pricing a 95% chance of a hike by December, up from 67% before the release, and a meaningful risk of tightening as early as September. The release landed just weeks after RBA minutes revealed a divided board, with “several” members favouring a pre‑emptive hike to counter upside risks from housing, food and surging fuel prices.
Wednesday’s report also showed annual headline inflation came in at 3.5% compared with a forecast 3.3%. The largest contributor to annual inflation in July was housing, which rose 5%, followed by food and non-alcoholic beverages, up 3.2%. On a monthly basis, automotive fuel prices rose 7.5% in July after falling for three months in a row
The report is the final inflation print before the RBA’s Sept. 28–29 meeting and adds pressure on policymakers who paused rates in August to await further evidence. Analysts warn the July CPI “leaves little room” for the central bank to maintain its hold stance, especially as headline inflation also overshot expectations at 3.5% and housing costs jumped 5%. Still, signs of cooling in the labour market — including rising unemployment — complicate the picture, and next week’s GDP data will be critical in assessing whether the economy can absorb another rate increase. With global energy shocks feeding domestic prices and data centre investment adding to demand, the RBA now faces a narrow path: act quickly to contain inflation or risk falling further behind its target after nearly five years above the midpoint.
Hong Kong To Unveil Its First Five-Year Plan With Policy Address
Hong Kong will release its debut five-year plan on the same day Chief Executive John Lee delivers his annual policy address, as the financial hub seeks to align with longer term national planning. Lee will present the 2026-2030 masterplan at a Legislative Council meeting on Sept. 16 before delivering his policy address, the government said in a Wednesday statement. He will face lawmakers in a question-and-answer session the following day. The five-year plan is a first for Hong Kong, long known as a bastion of free markets and limited government intervention. It is intended to better sync the city’s priorities with mainland China’s 15th Five-Year Plan, while retaining an approach officials called “market-led and government-guided” in a consultation document.
Speaking to reporters after the visit, Lee noted that the arrangement is to make it easier for the public to understand the government’s policy direction. “The arrangement is to make it easier for people to understand how the five-year plan and the Policy Address are closely connected and share a continuous, coherent relationship,” he said. “By reading the five-year plan together with the Policy Address, people will be able to better understand how the government will adhere to the direction and strategies set out in the five-year plan, turning the blueprint into policy measures and move forward.” Lee said he will set out various performance indicators in this year’s Policy Address as “annual milestones”.
Singapore Manufacturing Output Growth At 5-Month Low
Singapore’s manufacturing production grew by 6.8% year-on-year in July, slightly above market forecasts for a 6.9% gain but easing from a 7.5% rise in June. The latest reading marked the softest growth since February, largely driven by weaker output growth in electronics (11.2% vs 21.1% in June), particularly in semiconductors (8.0% vs 20.8%) and other electronic modules & components (2.5% vs 5.5%). On a seasonally adjusted monthly basis, manufacturing output increased 2.3% in July, reversing a 7.2% decline in June. Considering the first seven months of the year, manufacturing output increased 9.8% from the same period a year earlier.
Bank of Thailand Leaves Policy Rate Unchanged
The Bank of Thailand left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 1% at its monetary policy meeting yesterday, in a unanimous decision, as the central bank maintained an accommodative stance to support the recovery. The Thai economy is projected to expand broadly in line with previous assessments in 2026 and 2027, supported by stronger-than-expected merchandise exports and private investment linked to the technology and AI cycle. However, growth remains low and uneven, while private consumption was weaker as households remained cautious amid rising living costs. Meanwhile, headline inflation is projected to be lower than assessed, mainly due to lower energy prices, but is expected to rise through the first quarter of 2027 due to El Niño and gradual cost pass through. Inflation is then expected to return to low levels amid weak domestic demand and below-potential growth.
The Fed’s Preferred Inflation Gauge Rises More Than Expected
July’s personal consumption expenditures price index — a monthly report detailing changes in prices of goods and services and the Federal Reserve’s preferred metric of inflation — showed a month-over-month and year-over-year increase of 0.2% and 3.7%, respectively. Both figures were 0.1% above what economists polled by Dow Jones had expected. However, core PCE, which excludes food and energy prices, came in as expected with a gain of 0.2% on the month and 3.3% annually.
The report also showed that personal income rose 0.4% while spending increased 0.2%, both stronger than expected. Goods prices actually declined on the month, off 0.1%, driven by a 2.7% decrease in gasoline and other energy-related goods and a 0.9% drop in furnishings and long-lasting household equipment. Services prices rose 0.3%, pushed by a 1.2% increase in financial services and insurance as well as a 0.3% gain in housing.
The report comes with Fed officials weighing their next policy move as inflation, despite generally soft monthly readings this summer, is still well above the central bank’s 2% goal. The rate setting Federal Open Market Committee will gather next on Sept. 15-16. Markets are pricing in only about a 1 in 3 probability of a move then, with the best chance for a rate hike coming in December.
“Today’s mild upside inflation surprise and relative economic strength weren’t necessarily what investors —or the Fed — wanted to see. It wasn’t enough to shift the balance for September’s FOMC meeting,” said Ellen Zentner, chief economic strategist for Morgan Stanley Wealth Management.
US Economic Growth Slows To 1.5% In Q2
The US economy expanded at an annualized rate of 1.5% in the second quarter of 2026, slowing from 2.1% in the previous quarter and matching the preliminary estimate. Personal consumption expenditures surged 3.4%, the strongest increase since Q3 2025, driven by a 4.3% rise in goods spending and a 3.1% increase in services. Government spending fell 1.0%, dragged down by a 13.2% plunge in nondefense federal spending. Net exports also weighed on growth, as imports surged 12.5%, outpacing a 4.5% increase in exports.
South Korea Takes On China In Arctic Trade Route
South Korea has launched its first commercial test voyage through Russia’s Northern Sea Route, signalling Seoul’s intent to compete directly with China in the emerging Arctic shipping corridor that could reshape Asia‑Europe trade. The PanStar Acro’s 45‑day round trip from Busan to Europe marks a strategic bid to cut transit times by about 10 days compared with the Suez Canal and to bolster Busan’s status as a regional logistics hub, even as China races ahead with regular Arctic services. The NSR promises cheaper, faster exports and a potential lifeline for Busan’s struggling economy, but Korean operators must navigate Russian control of the route, Western sanctions pressure, insurance and financing hurdles, and unpredictable Arctic conditions. Seoul has secured tacit US approval for the voyage, yet officials acknowledge future punitive action remains possible. As policymakers weigh national interest against geopolitical sensitivities, the Arctic experiment has become a test of South Korea’s ability to secure new trade routes while managing the diplomatic fallout.
Liquidators Can Pursue PwC Globally Over Evergrande Collapse
A Hong Kong court has ruled that liquidators of the collapsed property giant Evergrande can pursue PwC International—the global umbrella of the Big Four network—alongside its Hong Kong and mainland China member firms for alleged audit negligence, a decision that could reshape how global accounting partnerships handle cross‑border liability. Deputy High Court judge Patrick Fung said it was “at least arguable” that PwC International owed Evergrande a duty of care, allowing discovery and interrogatories to proceed as liquidators seek US$8.4 billion in damages after regulators found PwC auditors failed to meet professional standards when signing off Evergrande’s accounts. The ruling threatens the Big Four’s long‑standing model of legally separate national firms, raising the prospect that financial and legal risks could spill across the global network. PwC’s Hong Kong and mainland affiliates have already paid substantial fines over Evergrande‑related failures, while the liquidators argue the umbrella organisation should also be held responsible for oversight lapses that enabled Evergrande to inflate revenues and pay out billions in dividends before its 2021 collapse. PwC International said it disagreed with the decision and is evaluating its legal options.
Hyundai Bets On US Hybrid Boom To Take On Toyota
Hyundai is making a major bet on a US hybrid boom as it moves to challenge Toyota’s dominance and offset sliding American EV sales. At its investor day, the world’s third‑largest carmaker unveiled an aggressive plan for 100 new models by 2030, including 58 launches in North America, where it expects hybrids to make up more than half of its sales. Hyundai’s US hybrid sales jumped 71% in the second quarter, driven by higher fuel prices and a market pivot that has caught Detroit’s Big Three flat‑footed. The company will also enter 18 new segments — including mid‑size pick‑ups — and roll out range‑extended EVs next year to counter the impact of cancelled tax credits. As competition from BYD and other Chinese rivals intensifies globally, Hyundai is boosting North American production capacity and local parts sourcing to navigate Trump‑era tariffs, while also pushing into robotics with plans to mass‑produce Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid robot in 2028. Despite the bold strategy, Hyundai shares slipped 3.1% in Seoul, reflecting investor caution over whether the group can defend margins in the US while struggling to compete in non‑US EV markets.
Asian Markets Mixed
Asia-Pacific markets closed mixed on Wednesday. Japan’s Nikkei 225 added 0.6% to end the trading day at 66,262. South Korea’s Kospi was up 1.0% to 6,808. Australia’s benchmark S&P/ASX 200 was 0.4% lower, ending the trading day at 9,128. In Mumbai, the BSE Sensex dropped 0.2% to 77,473. Asian chip stocks rose ahead of Nvidia earnings, with analysts expecting revenue to nearly double to US$92 billion.
SoftBank is talking with investment banks about a potential US$10 billion to US$20 billion bond offering to help refinance a loan for its investment in US tech giant OpenAI, Bloomberg News reported. The bond sale would add to a slew of fundraising by companies looking to deepen their reach into AI, despite concerns about growing credit risks. Shares of Softbank rose 1.5% in Tokyo.
China Stock Markets Higher
Chinese stock markets were broadly higher. On the mainland, the CSI 300 added 0.9% to 4,591 as investors awaited developments from the ongoing National People’s Congress Standing Committee meeting. The August 25–28 session is being closely watched for policy support following weak economic data and repeated pledges from policymakers to bolster growth.
In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng index rose 142 points, or 0.6%, to 25,653. The Tech Index was up 0.8%.
Jack Ma bought more than HK$600 million (US$76.5mn) worth of Alibaba shares in recent days, joining Chairman Joe Tsai and Chief Executive Officer Eddie Wu in acquiring company stock. Ma’s purchase, along with those of other senior executives, aims to reverse a major selloff and quell concerns about Alibaba’s growing spending on AI. Alibaba has pledged to spend more than 380 billion yuan over three years on AI, which is already eroding margins, while the company expects annualized revenue from AI products to near US$10 billion this quarter. Ma’s surprise move gave Alibaba’s stock a modest bump Wednesday. It climbed as much as 3.2%, recouping a portion of losses this week after Alibaba raised HK$80 billion in Hong Kong’s biggest follow-on share offering, signalling a determination to amass and spend vast sums to take global AI leadership. The big stock sale spurred concerns about Alibaba’s dwindling profitability as it taps company coffers to finance China’s most aggressive AI infrastructure and services rollout.
European Markets Flat
Europe’s stock markets were unchanged, with the regional Stoxx 600 flat on the day as the pan-continental index looks set to secure its fifth straight winning month. The UK’s FTSE 100 also closed almost unchanged. Travel, banking and mining stocks were the top performers. Oil and gas stocks dropped 0.7% as crude oil futures fell more than 1% on the potential for a deal between Iran and Oman to secure a safe transit route through the Strait of Hormuz.
European Central Bank Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel said interest rates must rise further due to upside risks to inflation from the conflict in the Middle East and a strong eurozone economy. Schnabel warned that consumer price growth is likely to exceed 2% for an “extended period” due to high energy costs, and that acting only when this feeds into wages would leave policymakers “behind the curve”. The ECB may need to raise rates again, with Schnabel saying, “at the current policy rate, inflation is unlikely to return to target over the medium term, and therefore further tightening will be necessary”.
US Stocks Little Changed
US stocks were little changed on Wednesday after the latest personal consumption expenditures price index reading revealed that inflation remains elevated and traders awaited results from Nvidia after the closing bell. The S&P 500 index closed around the flatline at 7,676. The Dow lost 114 points, or 0.2%, to finish at 53,464. The Nasdaq Composite declined 0.1% to settle at 26,130.
Meta Platforms was 1.1% higher after the company reached an US$18bn settlement with 48 state attorney generals over a lawsuit alleging that its social media apps harmed young users. As part of the settlement agreement, Meta will also make changes to its services, Facebook and Instagram, including a two-hour time limit for users under 18.
Nvidia shares rose in after-hours trading after the chip giant posted another quarter of record earnings. While the results beat Wall Street expectations for the 15th consecutive quarter, investors’ muted reaction reflects rising anxiety surrounding the viability of the artificial intelligence trade and fears about overspending on AI infrastructure. While up 12% this year, Nvidia shares were off 1.6% today in regular trading and recently closed lower for seven straight trading days until the slide ended Tuesday.
US Treasuries Lower After PCE
The 10-year Treasury yield was 2 bps higher after the core PCE inflation report came in as expected. The 2-year yield rose 4 bps to 4.21%.
A week after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent jolted markets with his plan to bring down US borrowing costs, the impact is becoming clearer. Yields have inched lower. The 10-year US yield stands at 4.65% after touching 4.75% last week. The 30-year yield, at 5.17%, is just 15 bps from the highest since 2007. Market moves suggest they would be higher absent the intervention. Traders say they know there is a big buyer in the market and are reluctant to stand in the way citing what is being called the “Bessent put” effect. With crude down about 7% in the past week, the bond rally looks like an oil-assisted move, rather than the durable shift Bessent wanted, says MLIV strategist Brendan Fagan. With midterm elections approaching, there’s more talk that Donald Trump and Bessent will attempt to drive long-term yields lower. Any sign from Fed Chairman Warsh that he’s on board with Bessent’s plan would give investors a risk-on signal, says Brent Kochuba of SpotGamma. “You can assume that Trump and Bessent are going to pump this thing,” he says.
US Dollar Slightly Higher After PCE Data
The greenback nudged higher Wednesday following headline US inflation data, which was higher than expected, although the core measure was in line with forecasts. The US Dollar Index was up 0.2% at 99.14, remaining in the narrow range it has traded in for the last week. “It is hard to escape the fact that the second Trump Presidency is delivering a weaker dollar than US economic performance, or Fed policy, would suggest,” Kit Juckes, chief FX strategist at Societe Generale, said in a note Tuesday. “Dollar strength will only return when (if) domestic data turn stronger and put pressure on the Fed to tighten.”
The Japanese yen was lower for a third day, falling 0.1% to ¥159.31. Markets are currently pricing in around an 80% probability that the BOJ will raise rates by 25 bps to 1.25% next month, up sharply from about 23% before the central bank’s July meeting. The offshore Chinese yuan was steady around Rmb 6.72 per dollar.
Gold Falls As Investors Digest Stronger US Data
Gold prices fell 1.4% to $4,594 an ounce on Wednesday, snapping a three-session winning streak, as investors assessed fresh US economic data for clues on the Federal Reserve’s interest rate path. The PCE price index rose 0.2% in July, above expectations for a 0.1% increase, while annual inflation reached 3.7% versus forecasts of 3.6%. Core PCE rose 0.2% month-over-month and 3.3% year-over-year, both in line with expectations.
Oil Falls For Third Day
Oil fell for a third day as geopolitical tensions eased, with Iran and Oman saying they had reached a deal on an “interim framework” to resume shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The two countries will negotiate a permanent route “within 30 to 60 days,” Tasnim reported. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his Omani counterpart Badr Albusaidi discussed the initiative to establish a “temporary joint maritime corridor”. Technical talks between Iran and Oman will continue with the aim of agreeing on a permanent maritime corridor and other issues related to the strait. International benchmark Brent crude futures for October delivery fell 0.8% to $87.84 a barrel, taking its decline this week to about 7%. US West Texas Intermediate futures for October settled at $82.23 per barrel. Oil fell more than 3% earlier in the session as the US relies on economic pressure against Iran rather than military strikes, easing fears for now that the adversaries will return to war.
Bitcoin Lower As Short Covering Rally Fades
Bitcoin was trading 0.5% lower Wednesday after briefly rising above $81,000 on Tuesday. The cryptocurrency was last trading at 78,400. The pullback paused a sharp rally that had pushed Bitcoin up more than 20% over three days, its strongest three-day gain since 2023.
Peter Lewis’ Money Talk Podcast
On Thursday’s “Peter Lewis’ Money Talk” podcast, I’ll be joined by Andrew Freris, the CEO of Ecognosis Advisory, and Alex Frew McMillan, a free-lance writer and Asia columnist for TheStreet.com. In the second part of the show, we look at some of the latest developments in emerging markets and FinTech with Yanan Wu, the Chairman and CEO of Surfin Group.

Wall Street has widely criticised Bessent’s surprise move last week to “at least double” the Treasury’s purchases of long-term US government debt, with investors saying it could undermine the agency’s credibility and work against the Fed’s ability to tame this year’s inflation flare-up.
